title: Why Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO
content_html:
Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO following the board's decision to reinstate him on November 23, 2026. (NYT)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Less than two weeks after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia amid revelations about his extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, the chipmaker’s board has unanimously voted to reinstate him.

Nvidia announced on Monday (November 23) that Huang would return as president, CEO and board member, reversing its earlier refusal to consider his reinstatement despite mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump, Silicon Valley executives and investors.

“Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA,” board chairman Harvey Jones said, adding that his reinstatement was in the best interests of the company’s shareholders, employees, partners and customers.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Trump, who had repeatedly called for Huang’s return, welcomed the reversal on Truth Social. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” he wrote.

Nvidia shares surged more than 30% in premarket trading following the announcement, according to Reuters. Huang, meanwhile, said he was “honored to return” and thanked the board, employees and supporters for their confidence.

Why did Trump push for Huang’s return?

Despite reportedly being informed twice by his advisers about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy, Trump has publicly expressed his support of the former Nvidia CEO and called him a “legend” in a social media post following his resignation.

The two have had a seemingly symbiotic relationship, with Trump seeing Nvidia as “essentially too big to fail”, according to a November 12 investigation by The New York Times. Nvidia’s success has been integral to the US’s continued position as the market leader in artificial intelligence, a sector central to Trump’s economic agenda.

Story continues below this ad

The NYT also reported that Trump saw Huang as a modern-day Henry Ford who was leading a technological revolution, and that he viewed the company’s fortunes as closely intertwined with those of the US economy and stock market. Trump was concerned that Huang’s removal could trigger an economic downturn.

More Explained | Jensen Huang’s scandal exposes Nvidia’s ‘key-man risk’. What does it mean?

Trump also has a personal financial stake in Nvidia: an analysis of his financial disclosures by The Washington Post found that he held between $13 million and $62 million worth of the chipmaker’s shares as of the end of August.

According to The NYT, Trump even called Huang on November 10, shortly before his resignation, and urged him to keep fighting for his job.

Huang’s friendship with Trump developed during the president’s second term, when Huang and his wife Lori attended a donor dinner at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in April 2025. That month, Nvidia announced plans to produce up to $500 billion worth of AI infrastructure in the US over four years. The White House hailed the announcement as the “Trump effect”, linking it to the Trump’s efforts to revive American manufacturing.

Story continues below this ad

Huang was soon invited to accompany the US President on his visit to West Asia, where major deals involving Nvidia chips were announced.

Huang also successfully lobbied to ease restrictions on advanced American chip sales to China, despite objections from senior administration officials. He argued that wider adoption of US technology would help America maintain its lead over China in AI. The administration subsequently permitted certain Nvidia chip sales to China, drawing criticism over national security risks.

Who else is on Team Huang?

Elon Musk (left) and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the US-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington on November 19, 2025. (Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times)

Elon Musk has warned that Nvidia could lose important business relationships following Huang’s departure.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote on X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Story continues below this ad

Huang himself has spoken about the importance of such relationships. In an interview earlier this year, he said Nvidia had worked with chipmaker TSMC for nearly three decades without a legal contract, with the two companies relying on mutual trust.

Fortnite-maker Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad have also backed Huang’s reinstatement. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called Huang “a personal hero of mine”, but declined to take a position on whether he should return, saying he did not know enough about the matter.

Also in Explained | Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy

The campaign has also drawn support from prominent Nvidia investors. In an open letter to the company’s board, Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker urged directors to keep “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang”.

Why is Nvidia’s board opposed to Huang’s return as CEO?

Huang said last week he would be honoured to return if the board considered it in the best interests of shareholders and employees. However, Nvidia has maintained that he resigned following disclosures of behaviour inconsistent with its code of conduct and standards.

Story continues below this ad

At the company’s earnings call on November 17, chairman Harvey Jones said: “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

The company’s independent investigation remains underway, while long-serving CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

The board has also established a committee to oversee national security and export-control compliance, as scrutiny grows over Nvidia’s dealings with China. Kress has sought to reassure investors that the company’s relationships with major customers and suppliers remain intact.

The concerns extend beyond corporate governance. On Sunday (November 22), The NYT reported that US intelligence had tracked Alice Huang’s contacts with China’s Ministry of State Security during her relationship with Jensen Huang. US authorities are also investigating whether advanced Nvidia chips obtained by companies connected to her were illegally diverted to China.

Story continues below this ad

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The controversy has divided investors over whether Huang’s return would restore confidence or expose the company to further risks. An institutional Nvidia shareholder, speaking anonymously to Reuters, expressed reservations about reinstating him before the investigations concluded, pointing to Apple and Microsoft as examples of companies that continued to prosper after the departure of influential leaders.

The divisions extend to the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previously called for an outside successor and criticised the Commerce Department’s handling of chip exports to China. On Sunday (November 22), he said the US government was seeking answers about Nvidia’s chip sales to China and who had overseen compliance under Huang’s leadership.

title: Ganga Water Treaty: Will the 1996 pact be renewed? Where India, Bangladesh stand
content_html:
The Farakka barrage. Photo: Partha Paul
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Less than three weeks before the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty officially lapses on December 12, representatives from India and Bangladesh met in Dhaka this weekend (November 21-22) for the 91st routine meeting of the India-Bangladesh Joint Committee.

Although there was no official word on whether discussions for renewing the 1996 bilateral treaty were held, some reports have indicated that Bangladesh appears to be agreeable to the prospect of renewing the pact instead of seeking a fresh agreement altogether.

How did the treaty come to be, what are its provisions, and where do both countries currently stand on renegotiating the terms of engagement? We explain.

From friction to friendship

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Tensions had brewed over sharing of the Ganga waters since the 1950s, when the Indian government proposed building a barrage at Farakka in West Bengal, some 18 km from what would become the international border between India and (then) East Pakistan. Construction began in 1961, and upon its completion in 1975, the Farakka barrage started diverting waters from the Ganga to the Hooghly river, flushing out the silt around the Kolkata port located on the latter and keeping it navigable for ships.

But throughout its construction, friction remained and reached a flashpoint in 1976 when Maulana Bhashani, an Awami League party legislator in (by then independent) Bangladesh, led the “Farakka Long March” against India’s water policies, demanding the demolition of the barrage, which he argued had resulted in the drying up of the Padma river (Ganga’s main distributary in Bangladesh) and subsequent desertification.

Also read | The next India-Bangladesh Ganges treaty must also protect the river

Although there were ad hoc agreements signed between the two countries throughout the next decade (1977, 1982, and 1985), none of them provided lasting solutions.

Finally, in December 1996, both countries under the leadership of Prime Ministers H D Deve Gowda and Sheikh Hasina signed the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty, instituting a 30-year framework for a flow-sharing mechanism during the annual dry season (January to May) and setting up a joint committee to monitor and implement the pact.

Story continues below this ad

Ganga Water Sharing Treaty: Terms of agreement

The treaty, hailed as a milestone in bilateral diplomacy at the time, established a three-tiered allocation system based on historical data of average flow during a 10-day period between 1949 and 1988.

Under the agreement, if the flow of water falls to or below the lower threshold of 70,000 cusecs (cubic feet per second, the unit to measure flow), the two countries would share the water equally. If the flow is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, then Bangladesh would be entitled to 35,000 cusecs and India was to keep the remaining flow. In the event of the upper threshold of 75,000 cusecs or more, India would get 40,000 and Bangladesh would receive the balance (see table).

Annexure I of the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty.

The aforementioned terms were subject to an additional clause: between March 11 and May 10 each year, both countries would receive a guaranteed 35,000 cusecs of water in alternate three 10-day periods.

Although it lacks a minimum guarantee clause, the treaty has an emergency provision: Article II(iii) states that “in the event flow at Farakka falls below 50,000 cusecs in any 10-day period, the two Governments will enter into immediate consultations to make adjustments on an emergency basis, in accordance with the principles of equity, fair play and no harm to either party”.

Story continues below this ad

For resolving disputes, the Joint Committee (consisting of an equal number of representatives nominated by both governments) would be primarily responsible, failing which it would be referred to the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC). The two countries had set up the JRC in 1972 as a bilateral mechanism to deliberate and manage water sharing for 54 shared rivers, of which only the Ganga is governed by a formal treaty as of today.

Sticking points

Over the years, the treaty has been criticised in both countries for not accounting for the future needs of rising populations in both countries, besides climate change-induced crises. Although the treaty provides for renewal by mutual consent at the end of the 30-year period, both sides have indicated a willingness to revisit the agreement’s terms.

News reports from last year suggested India was seeking an additional 30,000 to 35,000 cusecs during the March 11-May 10 period to meet its growing needs, and that the new treaty could be relatively shorter in duration, that is, 10 to 15 years. PTI reported that during a JRC meeting, Bangladesh had asked for a guaranteed release of 40,000 cusecs of water between February and May, besides a longer treaty renewal period and enhanced flood data sharing.

One point of contention has been Bangladesh’s demand to reinstate a minimum guarantee, similar to what was laid down in the 1977 ad hoc agreement. This provision guaranteed that Bangladesh received at least 80% of its scheduled allocation during certain lean-season periods, even when actual availability fell short.

Story continues below this ad

Nilanjan Ghosh, who heads Development Studies at the think tank Observer Research Foundation (ORF), wrote in a piece for the ORF website: “A fixed volumetric guarantee that remains binding irrespective of actual flows could impose an asymmetric burden of hydrological risk on the upstream country. India therefore cannot commit to such an impracticable demand. This could leave India bearing a disproportionate share of climate-induced shortages, regardless of its domestic needs.”

Also read | Why Bihar wants the Farakka treaty scrapped — and why it puts Centre in a bind

After the Tarique Rahman-led Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s landslide victory in the country’s general election in February 2026, reports had emerged that the treaty’s renewal would be among the top priorities of the newly elected government. But no discussions have been forthcoming on that front, even as tensions continue to simmer between the two countries over the contentious issue of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s extradition, who has been living in exile in New Delhi since her ouster in August 2024. It was understood to be why Tarique Rahman didn’t go ahead with a proposed official visit in August 2026 — it would’ve been his first since becoming prime minister.

The same month, the treaty’s provisions saw resistance brewing in Bihar, where the Janata Dal (United) — an ally of the BJP — pushed against its renewal, saying that the pact had proved “detrimental to Bihar’s interest”.

India’s decision last year to unilaterally put the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan in abeyance after the Pahalgam terror attack in April 2025 has also prompted caution in Bangladesh.

What next

Story continues below this ad

As to the way forward, Srinivas Chokkakula, president and chief executive of the New Delhi-based think tank Centre for Policy Research, said in a July 2026 op-ed for The Indian Express that the next treaty “presents an opportunity not merely to renew a bilateral water-sharing arrangement but to reimagine a regional strategic vision to address challenges of this new age of shared vulnerabilities and fragmented global economy”.

Chokkakula, who argued that the two countries would need to invest in appropriate processes and revisit existing bilateral institutions, wrote: “The changed realities and greater uncertainties, including water availability, will need robust and resilient transborder institutions to address the enhanced scope of issues — water sharing, data collection and monitoring, dispute resolution, responding to risks, etc. Finally, both countries will have to reinvent the political capital that made the 1996 treaty possible, and reinvest in it.”

title: Why Myanmar’s genocide verdict matters, including for Israel’s case
content_html:
The ICJ in Netherlands ruled that Myanmar committed genocide during its 2016-17 operations in Rakhine State (credit: Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has found that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar “committed genocide” against the Rohingya ethnic group in the country’s northern Rakhine State.

Announced on Thursday (November 19), the verdict makes Myanmar the first sovereign State in history to be directly held responsible for such a crime.

It comes 78 years after the UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, and 82 years after a Polish-Jewish lawyer, Raphael Lemkin, coined the term “genocide”.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is the relevance of this judgment, and can it have a bearing on other pending ICJ cases — including the one on Israel’s actions in Palestine?

Why holding a ‘State’ responsible for genocide is significant

The 1948 convention defines genocide as killing members of a group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction partially or wholly, imposing measures to prevent births within the group, and forcibly transferring their children to another group.

Also Read | Everyday Global: What is the International Court of Justice

Its adoption marked a unique development for international law governing State actions. In that decade, the most prominent international legal development was the codification of individual criminal responsibility, when Nazi German officials were held responsible after the Second World War (1939-45) for several ‘high crimes’ through a new body of international criminal law.

These laws were codified in the 1945 London Charter for the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, which listed three crimes: Crimes Against Peace, War Crimes, and Crimes Against Humanity. Nonetheless, both the ‘Nuremberg Trials’ as well as its successor ‘Tokyo Tribunal’ prosecuted individuals, and not States, for international crimes, despite the Holocaust being a genocide perpetrated as part of Nazi State policy.

Story continues below this ad

Even as the 1948 convention gave the ICJ jurisdictional authority to consider any State’s breach of the convention as a “crime under international law”, international legal opinion remained that only individuals could be held criminally responsible.

This was clear in the very first of the ‘Nuremberg Principles’: “Crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities, and only by punishing individuals who commit such crimes can the provisions of international law be enforced”.

Individual criminal responsibility remained unsettled for decades. How could an individual be charged for actions committed under the flag of a sovereign State?

Even when the State of Israel prosecuted Adolf Eichmann in 1961 for the Holocaust, Israeli judges had to draw parallels to the crime of international piracy to make the case that genocide was so grave a crime that any accused could be tried by any legal authority anywhere.

Story continues below this ad

The jurisprudence of such courts, building on the reasoning at Nuremberg and Tokyo, was eventually advanced by other courts across the last century.

Individual criminal responsibility for three crimes in particular — genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity — was advanced principally by the International Criminal Tribunals for Rwanda and Yugoslavia, before being codified in the 1998 Rome Statute for the International Criminal Court (which specifically prosecutes individuals).

For the ICJ, States remain outside the scope of criminal responsibility. This has meant that to even hold States guilty of breaching the 1948 convention, the court has historically applied a very strict legal threshold.

History of genocide cases at the ICJ

For the ICJ to conclusively find a breach of the 1948 Genocide Convention, two aspects must be present — actus reus or the physical act, and dolus specialis or the specific intent to commit the crime of genocide.

Story continues below this ad

The road to establishing such intent is especially narrow. Based on the ICJ’s own jurisprudence, “The Court may only establish genocidal intent by inference from circumstantial evidence if it is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence”.

Before Gambia v. Myanmar, the ICJ has ruled on two other cases involving the convention: Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007) and Croatia v. Serbia (2015). In the latter, the court did not find the existence of dolus specialis, dismissing both parties’ claims and counterclaims.

Also Read | Explained: The ICJ ruling on the genocide case against Israel for its actions in Gaza

In the former, however, the ICJ did indeed recognise the 1995 Srebrenica Massacre as genocide but held that Serbia’s main violation was failing to prevent individual perpetrators from committing genocide. It did not hold Serbia directly responsible.

Hence, even as the court has held a State responsible for breaching the 1948 convention’s obligations to prevent genocide, it has never held a State directly responsible for the act.

Story continues below this ad

Crucially, in both cases, the ICJ relied on the findings and reasoning already established by the Yugoslavia Tribunal to consider the presence/absence of dolus specialis.

In Gambia v. Myanmar, however, the ICJ’s reasoning was drawn principally from the facts submitted to it relating to this case alone. These included the submissions of the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar and the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar.

Their findings, amidst a vast evidentiary pool, were sufficient to pass the “only reasonable inference” test, allowing the court to hold Myanmar directly responsible for genocide under Article III of the 1948 convention.

Such direct responsibility is different from other crimes under the same Article, such as failing to prevent the commission of genocide (which the court also found Myanmar guilty of). Hence, the court did not dilute its strict legal threshold to establish dolus specialis for genocide.

The ICJ is not a Court of Record, as understood in the domestic sense for any country’s judicial system. It is not tied to its own past judgments; Article 59 of the ICJ Statute states that its judgments have “no binding force except between the parties and in respect of that particular case.”

The historic nature of the latest judgment itself was achieved through a rare 9-6 split amongst the 15 judges of the Bench, showing continued polarisation of opinion on direct State responsibility.

Collectively, this means that there is no predetermined implication of the 2026 judgment on other active cases relating to the 1948 Genocide Convention, such as South Africa v Israel (2023), in which Israel is accused of directly committing genocide in the Gaza Strip.

Most importantly, the court ruled that the presence of other counter-insurgency objectives during actus reus did not preclude the co-existence of genocidal intent.

In Gaza, Israel has committed similar actions at exponentially larger scales, justifying it as part of its counter-terror campaign against Hamas. title: NEET-2027: What reforms could be proposed, what more needs to be done
content_html:
The Nandan Nilekani-led high-powered task force must provide a time-bound implementation roadmap that defines institutional responsibilities, resources, technical safeguards, independent oversight, and accountability. Photo: Express
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Recurring controversies over the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) have exposed persistent vulnerabilities in India’s public examination system. The NEET-2024 examination, which saw paper leaks, exam malpractices, and candidates getting abnormal scores, led to the constitution of the Radhakrishnan Committee — whose 101 recommendations pertained to exam reforms.

Yet, the NEET-2026 examination in May was marked by allegations of paper leaks and cancellations, and the subsequent retest (Re-NEET) in June was followed by widespread student protests. Repeated and incorrect questions as well as answer-key discrepancies have further undermined confidence in competitive examinations.

In July 2026, the government constituted a Nandan Nilekani-led High-Powered Task Force (HPTF) to recommend comprehensive reforms in public examinations, including those conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA). Its initial deadline of October 2026 for submitting its report has been extended to January 2027 after receiving over 50,000 suggestions and extensive stakeholder consultations.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

With no interim report publicly available, NEET-2027 candidates face considerable uncertainty. With computer-based testing (CBT), a secure question vault, last-minute paper assembly, and digital delivery among the reported proposals, we look at what reforms are likely to be considered, their limitations and challenges, and what needs to be done to restore fairness and institutional accountability beyond NEET-2027.

Why have earlier reforms failed to prevent recurring NEET crises?

Following the NEET-2024 controversy, the Dr Radhakrishnan Committee recommended reforms covering examination security, technology, infrastructure and institutional processes.

But the NEET-2026 crisis raises questions about their implementation and oversight. Vulnerabilities exist across the examination chain — from question setting and review to transportation, storage, examination-centre management, and evaluation. Allegations of insider involvement make these particularly serious.

Story continues below this ad
Also read | Under paper leak shadow, NTA looks for spaces for exam centres; seeks AICTE support next year

New recommendations will have little value unless earlier failures are investigated, institutional responsibility is established, and proposed reforms are rigorously piloted.

Is CBT feasible for NEET?

CBT reduces dependence on physical printing, packaging, transportation, and storage, while enabling computerised administration, controlled access, and automated evaluation. But it introduces digital vulnerabilities, system failures, and cybersecurity risks.

A nationwide examination requires adequate centres, secure systems, reliable power and connectivity, trained personnel, and contingency arrangements. Uneven infrastructure and varying computer familiarity among candidates also raise concerns about accessibility and fairness.

CBT’s feasibility must be established through infrastructure assessment, large-scale pilots, and independent technical audits. Changing the examination format alone cannot guarantee security or fairness.

Story continues below this ad

Can a question vault and last-minute digital delivery secure the question paper?

Security must begin with question creation and validation, not merely paper transportation. Question setting, review, syllabus alignment, translation, and answer verification are all potential points of compromise, particularly with concentrated access.

A proposed question vault would maintain a large pool of independently vetted questions. The final paper could be assembled shortly before the examination, encrypted and digitally transmitted to centers, thereby reducing advance access and dependence on physical transport.

Candidates being screened as they arrive at an examination centre for the RE NEET UG exam in Jaipur on June 21, 2026. Photo: Rohit Jain Paras

The question paper repository, selection software, servers, encryption keys, and transmission networks require restricted access, traceable operations, and independent cybersecurity audits. Ultimately, security depends on the entire chain — from question setters and validators to final selection and delivery.

How can fairness be ensured across multiple CBT sessions?

Story continues below this ad

Multiple NEET sessions require different question papers, yet all candidates must compete on a common merit list. Ensuring equivalent difficulty is therefore a major challenge.

Statistical normalisation, potentially using percentile scores, may help compare performance. But its reliability depends on the comparability of the papers and on statistical assumptions. Even small adjustments can affect ranks and admission prospects.

Also read | NEET moving online: Education Ministry prepares CBT upgrade for future exams

Through rigorous pilots and independent validation, NTA must establish that papers have comparable syllabus coverage, difficulty, and discriminatory power. The methodology and its limitations must be transparent and auditable. Normalisation cannot compensate for fundamentally unequal question papers.

Beyond technical reforms, changes to eligibility, examination schedules, sessions, and format could further reduce vulnerabilities. Such changes require advance notification and phased implementation. In the absence of timely official announcements, major structural changes to NEET-2027 should be ruled out.

Can a two-stage NEET examination address normalisation concerns?

Story continues below this ad

A two-stage examination, on the lines of IIT-JEE (Mains and Advanced), is one possible alternative. All eligible candidates would appear in a screening examination (Mains), followed by a final examination for shortlisted candidates (Advanced) based on predefined cut-offs or a specified number of qualifiers. A single-session final examination does not need normalisation.

This model raises questions about shortlisting, eligibility, syllabus, question paper format and difficulty, scoring, and cut-offs. It would increase examination overheads but improve fairness in rankings for top scorers.

Should Class XII marks carry weightage in NEET? Can NEET be conducted twice a year?

On Tuesday (November 17), The Indian Express reported that providing weightage to Class 12 board exam scores in NEET-UG has emerged as a key proposal from several states during “consultative meetings” held so far with the Nilekani-led task force. Another proposal discussed was offering more than one attempt in a year.

Also read | States to Nandan Nilekani task force: Give weightage to Class 12 board exam scores in NEET UG

Weightage to Class XII marks could recognise sustained academic performance, but variations in board examinations and marking standards make equitable weightage difficult. Conducting NEET twice a year could offer candidates another opportunity to improve their scores, but would increase logistical costs and raise concerns about normalisation and admission timelines.

Story continues below this ad

A two-stage NEET, along the lines of IIT-JEE, could address both concerns: Class XII marks could be used in determining eligibility for the second-stage single-session examination.

Could the HPTF recommend changes to eligibility, attempts, or age limits?

With over two million candidates competing for limited medical seats, NEET’s unlimited attempts and the absence of an upper age limit raise questions about the examination’s capacity and the size of the candidate pool. Candidates can appear repeatedly, irrespective of age, even beyond 60.

Age limits and attempt restrictions, common in most competitive examinations, could help narrow the candidate pool.

Story continues below this ad

Can GenAI improve question generation and the quality of examinations?

Conventional software can select pre-vetted questions from a secure vault without GenAI. GenAI could assist in question generation, syllabus mapping, translation, preparing answer options, and calibrating difficulty, creating a larger, more diverse question pool.

Also read | CISF, AI monitoring, security experts: How NTA is changing after NEET leak

AI-generated questions, however, may contain factual errors, ambiguities, incorrect answer keys, syllabus errors, or translation defects. Expert validation is essential; AI may assist question development.

What should the HPTF deliver to restore confidence in public examinations?

Story continues below this ad

The Nilekani-led HPTF must provide a time-bound implementation roadmap that defines institutional responsibilities, resources, technical safeguards, independent oversight, and accountability. Major reforms must undergo large-scale pilots before nationwide implementation.

NTA also needs permanent expertise in examination management, cybersecurity, psychometrics, digital forensics, and vigilance. The HPTF’s success must ultimately be measured by whether examinations become secure, transparent, reliable, and fair. India needs not merely new examination technology but also trustworthy examination standard operating procedures and institutions.

The author is a former computer science professor at IIT Kharagpur, IIT Kanpur, BITS Pilani and JNU, and a former scientist at the Defence Research and Development Organisation and the Department of Science & Technology.

title: Why common infections are becoming harder to treat in India: ICMR scientist explains
Who keeps the internet running, and what happens when they can no longer afford to? An expert explains
content_html:
After the PHP2Shell flaws were disclosed, open-source maintainers helped get security fixes to users, including those on older PHP releases. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

When two critical security flaws in PHP, a programming language used by millions of websites, prompted organisations around the world to take services offline in October, Czech software engineer Ondřej Surý was among the maintainers who helped get the fixes to users.

The flaws, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, led to precautionary shutdowns on October 21 of services run by Japan’s Finance Ministry, US human-resources platform BambooHR, the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia.

Surý maintains widely used PHP software packages for Debian and Ubuntu, two Linux-based operating systems. He made patched versions available even for older releases of PHP that no longer receive official security updates.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Surý does much of this maintenance alongside his full-time job as Director of DNS Engineering at the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC), which develops software that helps translate website addresses into the numerical addresses computers use to communicate over the internet. He told The Indian Express that ISC had seen a sharp spike in vulnerability reports this year, although relatively few were serious. As AI tools make it easier to identify potential security flaws, assessing and fixing them still requires human expertise.

The experience raises a larger question about the sustainability of open-source software, whose underlying code is freely available for others to use, modify and distribute, and on which much of the internet depends. In an interview with The Indian Express, Surý discusses the PHP2Shell incident, the growing demands of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, and why he believes businesses that profit from open-source software must help fund its maintenance. Edited excerpts:

Why does PHP matter to the functioning of the internet, and what made the recent PHP2Shell vulnerabilities particularly serious?

PHP is a programming language mainly used to develop websites. Roughly 70% of the web is powered by PHP. The recently discovered vulnerabilities in PHP were in the most serious category, remote code execution (RCE). In short, an attacker can exploit such a vulnerability to execute a program of their own choosing on a remote machine, potentially gaining full access to the server (the computer running the website or service).

When researchers discover a serious security flaw in widely used software, what happens next? Who develops the fix, who ensures it reaches users, and which parts of this process still depend heavily on human work?

Story continues below this ad

When ethical security researchers discover a serious security flaw, they contact the affected project or organisation privately. Any project or organisation that cares about security should have a mechanism through which researchers can report flaws in its software.

Also in Explained | What is PHP2Shell, and why did it force websites around the world offline?

Fixing the vulnerability is usually no different from fixing any other defect in the software, but the process depends on the size of the project. The work could fall to a single person in a small project or a handful of people in a larger one. They might or might not be employed to do this work.

In the case of PHP, there are a handful of volunteers for whom this is a side project, and very few people are employed directly by the PHP Foundation. Most of the important work still depends on people. As for when and how AI is used, it is important to remember that AI is just a tool that might or might not be useful in specific cases.

How did the early disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affect the release of security updates?

Story continues below this ad

That was unfortunate because people who knew the original release schedule had made plans to properly release the software so that users could upgrade. The premature disclosure accelerated the whole process by a day.

Now, this is the bad part about AI: once details of the upcoming vulnerabilities were known, people started using AI to search for possible security flaws. It was no longer safe to stick to the original schedule because AI, as a tool, is quite good at finding security vulnerabilities, especially when guided by a skilled person.

AI tools are increasingly being used to discover vulnerabilities in software. Have you noticed any change in the number or complexity of vulnerability reports you receive, or in the work required to respond to them?

In my day job, I am the Director of DNS Engineering at ISC, responsible for BIND 9, a widely used open-source DNS server. There was a sharp spike this year in the frequency and depth of the vulnerability reports we received.

Story continues below this ad

Fortunately, after the initial surge, things went back to normal. We still receive occasional security reports, but only very few of them are serious enough to be handled as security vulnerabilities.

That is the thing with AI: it needs to be guided by an expert with domain knowledge. Otherwise, you often end up with serious-sounding reports about ordinary software bugs, or issues that are not even bugs.

Could AI also help maintainers identify security vulnerabilities themselves?

Not only that, maintainers can also use frontier AI models to find security vulnerabilities themselves. That said, both offensive (finding and exploiting vulnerabilities) and defensive (finding and fixing vulnerabilities) uses of AI need to be supervised by an expert. Otherwise, you might end up with a pile of mediocre-quality reports or, worse, AI might miss something serious.

You’ve spoken about the difficulty of sustaining open-source maintenance. Why does so much essential software depend on the work of relatively few people, and what would it take to support them adequately?

Story continues below this ad

When I joined university in 1995, free software was still very new, at least to me, and I found a purpose in making the fruits of my work freely available to others. It was a paradigm change, and I believe many people involved in the free-software movement are still driven by those ideals.

title: An expert explains why fixing India's air pollution crisis needs more than technical solutions
content_html:
A machine sprays water amid heavy air pollution in New Delhi on November 13. (Express photo by Amit Mehra)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Air pollution is often discussed as if it were primarily a problem of Delhi NCR and winters, but much of India experiences unhealthy air throughout the year, both outdoors and indoors.

North India faces particularly severe outdoor pollution episodes because of numerous emission sources and unfavourable winter meteorology. And every winter, experts are called upon to decode these phenomena — atmospheric scientists explain the meteorology, engineers discuss pollution control, and doctors warn about health impacts.

After over a decade of the problem visibly worsening, it is worth examining how this knowledge has helped understand the situation, the limitations of the current approach, and the kind of information and scientific research that are still required.

The problems and solutions are not particularly mysterious

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The sources of air pollution are known by now — fireworks and agricultural residue burning contribute during specific periods, while solid fuels such as firewood, dung cakes, and even waste are burnt for heating in colder months. Transport, polluting household fuels, waste burning, industry, power plants, and construction contribute year-round. Weather affects how emissions disperse and accumulate; it does not create them.

The major sources of pollution are well established, and we do not need to quantify every source precisely or measure every exposure before acting.

Fundamentally, reducing air pollution requires two clear actions: reducing the number of emitting sources and reducing emissions from those that remain. This means reliable public transport and less dependence on private vehicles, access to clean cooking and heating, viable alternatives to crop residue burning, functioning municipal waste management, and effective industrial regulation.

Stubble burning and firecrackers receive considerable attention during particular periods, but even addressing these requires looking beyond the immediate pollution episode and avoiding purely technological fixes.

Story continues below this ad

Agricultural residue burning cannot be addressed without understanding farming practices, farmers’ economic constraints, and the availability of alternatives. Similarly, reducing pollution from firecrackers requires not only restrictions and enforcement, but also changing social attitudes, with schools, communities, and religious and spiritual leaders playing a role.

Neither problem can be solved by atmospheric scientists or enforcement agencies alone.

The relevance of scientific research

Uncertainties about source contributions, emission inventories, and atmospheric chemistry will always remain, to an extent, and sustained investment in science and monitoring remains essential. Our understanding of air pollution is indeed shaped by what we measure. Monitoring networks, emission inventories, and source apportionment studies help identify pollution sources for targeted policies.

Expert Explains | COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya

It must also be noted that what we measure in the ambient atmosphere is not necessarily what people breathe. For instance, a rooftop monitor or a model forecast does not tell us the particulate matter levels inside a home while someone cooks with solid fuels. For those households relying on solid fuel for cooking and heating, household air pollution remains a major part of daily exposure. It additionally contributes to outdoor air pollution.

Story continues below this ad

But research should help refine interventions, not become a prerequisite for starting them. We do not need to know the precise contribution of every source before acting on those already identified.

We need greater attention to studying personal exposure, particularly among the most vulnerable sections of society, but these gaps should not obscure what we already know. The solutions we need are often not those for which we lack expertise; they are those that lack institutional attention, political commitment, and sustained investment.

The question of expertise

This brings us to a more fundamental question: who exactly is an air pollution expert? The obvious answers are atmospheric scientists studying aerosols and meteorology, engineers developing pollution controls, doctors treating respiratory disease, and epidemiologists studying long-term health impacts.

Recognition of expertise is also shaped by institutional affiliation. Scholars from IITs and AIIMS may command immediate recognition, while equally valuable knowledge from less prominent institutions and practitioners working on the ground often receives less attention.

Story continues below this ad
Opinion | What the AQI isn’t telling you about air pollution

What about the agricultural economists studying farmers’ incentives, urban planners shaping transport systems, social scientists examining household energy choices and public behaviour, municipal officials responsible for waste management, and public health experts translating scientific evidence into preventive interventions?

Expertise is often recognised most readily when it comes with a technological solution. A new device is visible and presented as innovation, often as a silver bullet for a complex problem. More long-term, institutional and procedural changes, such as improving public transport, managing waste, or ensuring access to clean household energy, are less spectacular. They require sustained funding, institutional capacity, coordination, and often confronting vested interests.

Technological spectacle also raises the question of who scrutinises the claims made by those offering solutions. Every winter, proposals for smog towers, artificial rain, and other interventions are presented with considerable fanfare, despite questions about their effectiveness and scale. Such projects can consume substantial public resources, create lucrative opportunities for entrepreneurs, and offer governments the optics of action without meaningfully reducing emissions.

We need independent scientific scrutiny, as well as journalists, regulators, and civil society willing to question how public money is spent. Expertise must go beyond simply proposing solutions, and involve interrogating them as well.

Story continues below this ad

We should also consider those living and working with the highest pollution exposure: street vendors, construction workers, sanitation workers, farmers, communities alongside industrial facilities, and women who spend hours cooking with polluting fuels. Exposure is often shaped by the work people do and the choices available to them. For someone dependent on daily wages, earning a livelihood may take precedence over concerns about pollution.

Similarly, household cooking is often borne disproportionately by women, whose exposure is rarely reflected in ambient air quality measurements. Effective interventions must therefore consider safer working conditions, viable livelihood alternatives, access to clean household energy, and better economic opportunities.

As an atmospheric scientist, I would argue that we need more science, not less. Understanding the atmosphere, however, is not the same as understanding everything that makes it polluted. We must continue filling knowledge gaps without delaying action on what we already know. The priority must be to translate that knowledge into cleaner transport, energy, waste management, and effective regulation. The real test of expertise is not how spectacular a solution sounds, or how prestigious the institution linked to the expert proposing it is, but whether it helps make the air cleaner for everyone.

Shahzad Gani is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Atmospheric Sciences, IIT Delhi.

title: Balendra Shah visits India: What is on the table, from security to AI to cricket
content_html:
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen Shah, is in India on his first bilateral visit abroad since taking office in March. He will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi for bilateral talks on Monday, in their first in-person meeting.

Nepal’s Prime Ministers generally make their first visit to India, and quite early in their tenure. Yet, much is unusual about this visit, starting with the PM himself.

Advertisement

‘Nepal first’ PM

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician Balen Shah came to power on the back of massive youth protests, promising a break from Nepal’s old politics of patronage and dependence on regional big powers.

Shah was known for his administrative skills and development work as the Kathmandu Mayor. After taking the top office, in an effort to project difference from the old guard, Shah told ministers and officials to focus on domestic issues. He went so far as to issue a diktat: no foreign visits and no meetings with senior officials and ministers from other countries, unless with a President or a Prime Minister.

Thus, when US envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor visited Kathmandu in April-early May, Shah’s office did not schedule a meeting with him. Around the same time, the visit of India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri to Kathmandu was cancelled as Shah did not agree to a meeting.

Advertisement

Then, Shah said both India and Nepal had encroached on each other’s territory, and sought the involvement of China and UK to address the dispute, something India strongly rejected.

Also in Explained | History of India and Nepal’s border issue

The June visit of Shishir Khanal, Nepal’s Foreign Minister, and Rabi Lamichhane, the chief of Shah’s party, Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), smoothened matters and paved the way for Shah’s visit. His visit is being seen as an acknowledgement in Nepal of the need for continued engagement with India.

The strategic logic for engagement is clear as daylight: India is Nepal’s largest trade, transit and investment partner, Nepal enjoys duty-free access to the Indian market, and India is Nepal’s biggest export destination, receiving about 80% of Nepal’s goods exports. India is also the largest source of foreign investment in Nepal, accounting for almost 1/3rd of the total FDI received by the country.

Thus, even as Shah seeks to differentiate himself from his predecessors, there are key areas of cooperation which India and Nepal will look at.

Key areas of economic cooperation between India and Nepal

Energy: Bilateral cooperation in the power sector has been on an upward trajectory, with developments like the agreement for long term power trade that envisages the import of up to 10,000 MW power from Nepal to India over a period of 10 years. India currently imports about 1200 MW of power from Nepal annually.

Indian entities are involved in the development of several hydropower projects in Nepal, including the 900 MW Arun-3 Hydroelectric project under construction.

Energy supplies to Nepal were made more efficient and effective through a cross-border petroleum pipeline commissioned in 2019 between Motihari and Amlekhgunj. Phase-2 of this pipeline has also been implemented. Both sides are now exploring the development of new pipelines and terminals, and Balen Shah’s visit will look into this aspect.

Innovation ecosystem and AI: With Shah representing the youth, the start-up culture is a major area that India is likely to focus on.

Since 2025, several Nepali startups have received training through the India-Nepal Startup Partnership Network (IN-SPAN) in collaboration with IIT Madras and its Incubation Centre Pravartak.

Both sides are working to establish a collaborative framework for advancing Language AI, digital public infrastructure, and inclusive digital ecosystems across India and Nepal.

Education: For the first few decades after Indian independence, a majority of Nepal’s senior leaders were educated at Banaras Hindu University (BHU). But in recent years, Nepal’s youngsters are choosing Australia, Europe, Thailand, Singapore, and Dubai.

Scholarships provided by India for Nepali nationals provide extensive coverage, from school education to the Doctorate level, with 1,500 annual scholarships.

With Shah seen as the voice of the youth, the Indian government and Nepal are looking at the possibility of an IIT campus in Nepal.

Sports: Cricket has found huge enthusiasm among the Nepalese youth. In the past three years, there has been growth in the India-Nepal partnership in sports cooperation, particularly in cricket. In fact, the Nepal Premier League is said to be a huge money spinner, next to India’s IPL.

Tourism: India is the largest source of foreign tourists to Nepal. The data of air arrivals in the last Nepali financial year reflected 311,000 Indian visitors. This does not include the large number of visitors arriving by road. Both sides are thus working to promote shared circuits such as the Ramayana Circuit and the Buddhist Circuit.

The new direct passenger train services between Janakpurdham and Ayodhya, whose trial run was on November 5, will further facilitate religious tourism between India and Nepal.

India and Nepal already enjoy extensive cooperation in culture. Indian pilgrims visit Pashupatinath, Muktinath, Janaki Mandir and Lumbini, while Nepali pilgrims travel to Kashi, the Char Dham, Bodh Gaya and the Kumbh.

India-Nepal border management question

The most challenging issue during the visit is likely to be border management. While India and Nepal have contested some border areas for decades, in 2020, under former prime minister KP Oli, Nepal officially issued a new political map, showing Kalapani, Limpiadhura and Lipulekh in Uttarakhand as its territory. This locks all Nepal’s Prime Ministers in a position they find difficult to walk back from. Also, China has long sought a larger influence in Nepal, including over its boundary issues.

However, despite the differences, India and Nepal enjoy robust ties in defence and security. With the issue of Agniveers being resolved — by giving them a pathway for permanent commission — some misgivings among the Gorkha soldiers have been assuaged. India and Nepal also cooperate closely in areas such as countering narcotics, cross-border crimes, money laundering etc.

Balen Shah’s visit to India will be a key moment for a reset in the relationship. The effort is to bring the ties back on track, with a new PM who has been vocal about not being “pro-India” or “pro-China”, but “pro-Nepal”. The political establishment in Nepal is new and different from what India has dealt with, but their aspirational and ambitious political language is what India speaks, and well understands.

While India and Nepal have contested some border areas for decades, in 2020, under former prime minister KP Oli, Nepal officially issued a new political map, showing Kalapani, Limpiadhura and Lipulekh in Uttarakhand as its territory. This locks all Nepal’s Prime Ministers in a position they find difficult to walk back from. Also, China has long sought a larger influence in Nepal, including over its boundary issues.
However, despite the differences, India and Nepal enjoy robust ties in defence and security. With the issue of Agniveers being resolved — by giving them a pathway for permanent commission — some misgivings among the Gorkha soldiers have been assuaged. India and Nepal also cooperate closely in areas such as countering narcotics, cross-border crimes, money laundering etc.
Balen Shah’s visit to India will be a key moment for a reset in the relationship. The effort is to bring the ties back on track, with a new PM who has been vocal about not being “pro-India” or “pro-China”, but “pro-Nepal”. The political establishment in Nepal is new and different from what India has dealt with, but their aspirational and ambitious political language is what India speaks, and well understands.

title: How India’s first indigenous bird flu vaccine was developed, why it matters
content_html:
The bird flu vaccine, which costs Rs 1-2 per dose, was announced by Union Agriculture Minister and former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan in Bhopal on Friday. Photo: PTI
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

For years, India has dealt with recurring outbreaks of bird flu, caused by the highly pathogenic H5N1 strain of avian influenza. While the disease has primarily affected poultry, the virus has increasingly been detected in other animal species, including tigers, leopards, and other mammals. It has also infected humans, raising concerns about its potential to pose a wider public health threat.

Now, scientists at the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD) in Bhopal have developed India’s first indigenous vaccine against H5N1 for chickens. The vaccine, which costs Rs 1-2 per dose, was announced by Union Agriculture Minister and former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan in Bhopal on Friday (November 20).

We explain why the vaccine was needed, the challenges involved in developing it, and what the trials established.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Why India needed a bird flu vaccine

India’s first bird flu outbreak was reported in 2006 in Navapur, Maharashtra. Since then, the country has recorded more than 500 outbreaks, according to figures shared by Chouhan. Outbreaks have resulted in large-scale deaths and culling of poultry, affecting farmers and the wider poultry industry.

The vaccine targets a particular genetic group of the virus known as H5N1 Clade 2.3.2.1a, which has been responsible for a majority of bird flu outbreaks in Indian chickens since 2011.

A clade is a genetic grouping of viruses that share a common ancestry. H5N1 is the name of the virus subtype, while 2.3.2.1a identifies a particular genetic lineage within it. This is important because influenza viruses continue to change over time, and vaccines need to be suited to the strains circulating in a population.

Also read | Why Maharashtra’s poultry farmers are seeking bird flu vaccination

Dr S Nagarajan, principal scientist at NIHSAD who led the team of scientists involved in the vaccine’s development, told The Indian Express, “These outbreaks have caused huge economic loss to the poultry industry… Hence, the vaccine is important to control the clade 2.3.2.1a H5N1 virus strain to mitigate the economic losses to the farmers and to prevent emergence of a human pandemic virus.”

Story continues below this ad

The concern over this particular clade extends beyond poultry. “Outbreaks involving the same viral group were reported in several mammalian species, including tigers, lions, domestic cats, leopards and jungle cats in 2025,” Nagarajan said. According to him, three human deaths involving H5N1 viruses belonging to the same clade were also reported from Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, and Karnataka.

The vaccine is intended to protect chickens, not humans. Its potential public health benefit lies in reducing the circulation of the virus among birds and, consequently, the opportunities for transmission to people who come into contact with infected poultry.

Challenges in development of the vaccine

The vaccine was developed at ICAR-NIHSAD, an institute in Bhopal specialising in the diagnosis, surveillance, and research of high-risk animal diseases.

The institute has been working on avian influenza for years. Its research includes monitoring the different strains circulating in India, studying how the virus changes, and examining its ability to infect different animal species.

Story continues below this ad
Veterinary officials and other staff engaged in culling of birds in Navapur in Maharashtra’s Nandurbar district in February 2021. Photo: Deepak Joshi

Nagarajan said the biggest challenge was the time taken to develop the vaccine. “It took a lot of dedicated efforts and hard work to develop this vaccine. The biggest challenge was racing against the time to develop the vaccine within the minimum possible time,” he said.

The demands of the work also extended beyond the laboratory. Officials said the scientists worked through weekends and holidays and followed strict biosafety protocols throughout the research period. These included sanitisation procedures before and after leaving the laboratory, extensive bathing procedures and restrictions on keeping pets at home to minimise the possibility of carrying infection outside the facility.

How effective is the vaccine?

The vaccine has passed safety, efficacy, and potency tests in accordance with the prescribed guidelines of the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). According to Nagarajan, experimental trials showed that it provided 100% protection against the targeted H5N1 clade throughout the 24-week observation period following booster vaccination.

The 24-week finding, however, refers to the period observed after the booster dose under experimental conditions. Further details about the number of birds involved, the trial design, and performance under commercial farm conditions would help establish the vaccine’s efficacy when used on a larger scale.

Story continues below this ad
Also read | Bird flu outbreak in Maharashtra: How it infects humans and why experts are on alert

Another important finding was that the vaccine prevented the transmission of the virus between chickens. In the trials, vaccinated chickens were kept in contact with unvaccinated birds. The researchers found that the vaccinated birds did not transmit the virus to their unvaccinated counterparts.

This is important because a vaccine that protects individual birds from developing severe disease can reduce deaths on poultry farms. Preventing transmission can also help limit the circulation of the virus among birds and reduce the risk of further outbreaks.

What does it mean for poultry farmers?

The vaccine has been priced at Rs 1-2 per dose, making it relatively inexpensive for poultry farmers. Its intended use is to protect chickens, particularly layers and growers, against clinical disease and deaths.

Layers are chickens raised for egg production, while growers are birds being raised towards maturity. Preventing infection in these populations could help farmers avoid losses and disruptions to production.

Story continues below this ad
At a chicken market in New Delhi in July 2021. Bird flu outbreaks have resulted in large-scale deaths and culling of poultry. Photo: Praveen Khanna

Nagarajan said that properly administered vaccination would protect chickens against clinical signs and deaths and prevent transmission to unvaccinated birds. It could also reduce environmental contamination by limiting the circulation of the virus.

The vaccine, however, is not yet available for farmers to use commercially. The next step is the transfer of technology to manufacturers who can produce it at scale and make the vaccine available to poultry farmers. Nagarajan said that transfer of technology “will be initiated at the earliest possible” and the time for actual vaccine availability will depend on the process proposed by the Centre’s Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying.

What does this mean for India’s animal disease research?

NIHSAD has previously developed indigenous vaccines for diseases including Gumboro, Brucella abortus, Classical Swine Fever, and African Swine Fever. Its research also covers disease surveillance, diagnostics, and the study of pathogens that can spread between animals and humans.

Story continues below this ad

The H5N1 vaccine adds to this work by giving India a vaccine specifically developed against the clade responsible for most outbreaks in its poultry population.

Nagarajan said India was not dependent on other countries for vaccines against animal and bird diseases. The achievement, therefore, is not about ending dependence on foreign vaccines but developing a vaccine suited to a particular strain circulating in India.

title: Rahul Gandhi on Israel: How defence tech, Kargil war shaped India’s ties
content_html:
Lok Sabha LoP Rahul Gandhi during an open question-and-answer session with students and faculty, at University of Chicago, USA. (@INCIndia/X via PTI Photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Lok Sabha Leader of the Opposition and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi spoke this week about India needing to maintain its relationship with Israel due to “strategic reasons”.

Gandhi condemned Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attacks and Israel’s actions against Palestinians, while adding that he supported a “strong relationship” with Israel. “We have strategic interests, including buying the best weapons for our armed forces. But that cannot mean silence on Gaza,” he said.

The comments come at a time when Israel has received global criticism, including from its longstanding ally, the United States. They also differ from the stronger, more critical stance adopted by key members of the Congress Party so far.

India’s foreign policy must be guided by what is good for India.

I support a strong relationship with Israel. We have strategic interests, including buying the best weapons for our armed forces. But that cannot mean silence on Gaza.

I condemn the October 7th attacks and the killing of innocent people. I also condemn what Israel has done in Gaza. One wrong cannot justify another.

We are a nation of 1.5 billion people. No country – Israel, USA, Russia or China – should hold us back from playing our rightful role on the global stage.

India must stand for what it believes in.

— Rahul Gandhi (@RahulGandhi) November 19, 2026

India has historically supported the cause of Palestinian statehood, even as it has, of late, deepened relations with Israel. A key factor in this trajectory is defence ties, and one milestone was the 1999 Kargil War. Over the years, The Indian Express has extensively reported on and explained the history and the shifts. This article brings together those explainers to provide a one-stop guide.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Where India stood on Israel, Palestine historically

As The Indian Express earlier reported on India-Israel ties, India recognised the State of Israel soon after it was created in 1948. The establishment of full diplomatic relations would take four more decades, influenced by how national leaders perceived the issue at the time.

Jawaharlal Nehru and Mahatma Gandhi opposed the creation of a State based on religion — a view in line with their opposition to the Partition of India. India’s position with regard to Palestine was also guided by the consensus in the Arab world, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the United Nations.

On January 10, 1975, India recognised the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) as the sole and legitimate representative of the Palestinian people and permitted it an independent office in New Delhi.

Also Read | Mahatma Gandhi’s views on Israel, Palestine

Notably, this stance was retained during the first non-Congress government at the Centre in 1977, led by the Janata Party. Addressing a public meeting arranged by the Indo-Arab Friendship League on January 28, 1978, then External Affairs Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee asked the Non-Aligned Movement and all those who believed in peace and justice in the world to “raise their voice in protest against the injustice being meted out to Palestinians”.

Story continues below this ad

India’s changing ties with Israel

Former West Asian studies professor PR Kumaraswamy earlier wrote that over time, factors like the Cold War’s end and the willingness of Arab countries to negotiate peace, as well as India obtaining arms from Israel during the 1962 China War and the Indo-Pakistani wars in 1965 and 1971, hinted at a sense of “shared security” with Israel.

Following his 1984 electoral victory, Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi initiated some contacts with Israel, which “became an integral part of the pragmatic, non-ideological approach to foreign policy pursued by Narasimha Rao.”

As earlier reported, the Arab countries’ neutral position during the 1962 war and their support for Pakistan in later conflicts did not go down well with many, including the BJP. Things changed in West Asia when Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990. The PLO lost its political leverage on account of its support for Saddam Hussein. Around that time, the Soviet Union disintegrated, and this prompted India to make drastic changes in its policy towards West Asia.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was in India on January 19-20, 1992. During a meeting with Prime Minister P V Narasimha Rao, he was told that India’s establishment of the relationship with Israel would be helpful for the Palestinian cause. He was told that New Delhi could exert influence on Israel only if it had an ambassador in Tel Aviv. Arafat came on board.

Story continues below this ad

He then famously told a press conference in New Delhi: “Exchange of Ambassadors and recognition (of Israel) are acts of sovereignty in which I cannot interfere… I respect any choice of the Indian government”. This would prove to be a game-changer. India formally established diplomatic ties with Israel on January 29, 1992, around 10 days after Arafat’s public approval.

The defence factor in India-Israel ties

By the time of the Kargil war in 1999, full diplomatic ties with Israel came in handy. The Indian Air Force (IAF) desperately needed precision bombs to target Pakistani intruders hiding in the caves and bunkers in Kargil’s mountains. After political approvals, IAF leaders reached out to their Israeli counterparts, who wasted no time. Israel is understood to have dug into its emergency stockpiles and shipped them to India’s air bases within days.

Also Read | Israeli help and Indian jugaad in recapture of Tiger Hill

In his visit in 2015 to Israel, then President Pranab Mukherjee had acknowledged and appreciated Israel’s support during the war and thanked it for providing “critical defence supplies”.

India responded to this decisive show of support by organising a series of high-profile visits to Israel in 2000, with external affairs minister Jaswant Singh leading the first-ever Indian bilateral visit to the country. Home Minister L K Advani also visited that summer.

Story continues below this ad

More recently, India has been the biggest purchaser of Israeli weapons over the last decade, especially between 2015 and 2019, including drones, missile systems, sensors, surveillance technology and border-control equipment.

title: Why Cyclone Akvan in Bay of Bengal contributed to early fog in Punjab, Haryana
content_html:
A foggy evening in Hoshiarpur on November 21. (Express photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Winters in Punjab are usually dominated by conversations around smog and stubble-burning. This November, however, another winter phenomenon is attracting attention: early fog.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD), Chandigarh, has forecast dense fog at isolated places in Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh from November 19 to 22, weeks before prolonged winter fog normally becomes a regular feature of the northern plains in December and January.

Why is Punjab seeing a foggy November?

Meteorologists attribute the early fog to moisture incursion, light north-westerly winds, atmospheric stability, and night-time cooling. The cyclonic system over the Bay of Bengal is also influencing the larger circulation and moisture pattern.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Fog forms when air near the ground cools to its dew point, the temperature at which moisture in the air condenses to form water droplets. Thus, adequate moisture in the lower atmosphere is as essential as cooling.

Minimum temperatures have been below normal at several locations in Punjab, though the pattern is not uniform. According to IMD Chandigarh observations on November 19, Chandigarh recorded 10.4°C (1°C below normal), Patiala 9.3°C (-2°C), Hisar 10°C (-2°C), Narnaul 9.5°C (-2°C) and Rohtak 10.6°C (-1°C).

This variation is significant because fog is localised: dense patches can form where moisture, surface cooling and weak winds coincide, even as nearby stations record normal or above-normal temperatures.

Also in Explained | Why counting farm fires is not enough to measure the scale of stubble burning

Surinder Pal, director, IMD Chandigarh, said moisture availability, weak winds and falling night temperatures were creating favourable conditions. The IMD’s November 19 bulletin also noted a weak western disturbance, with a trough (an elongated area of relatively low atmospheric pressure) in the middle layers of the atmosphere over eastern Afghanistan and north-west Pakistan.

Story continues below this ad

Why can fog be dense in some areas while nearby areas are clear?

While moisture provides the essential ingredient for fog, light winds and atmospheric stability determine its formation and persistence. Surinder Pal said moisture incursion, along with light north-westerly winds, was creating favourable conditions. Weak winds restrict the mixing and dispersal of air near the surface, allowing moisture to accumulate.

As the ground loses heat through radiation at night, the air above it cools. Once it reaches saturation, water vapour condenses into droplets. Stable atmospheric conditions restrict vertical mixing, allowing radiation fog to develop and persist, particularly during the night and early morning.

Local variations in humidity, irrigation, canals, agricultural fields, vegetation and surface temperatures explain why fog can be dense in isolated locations while nearby areas remain relatively clear.

Is Cyclone Akvan also influencing fog formation in north India?

The Severe Cyclonic Storm Akvan is another factor influencing the prevailing weather pattern. Surinder Pal pointed to its influence on moisture incursion. Cyclonic systems can alter atmospheric circulation and moisture movement over large areas, although Akvan should not be considered the sole or direct cause of fog in Punjab and Haryana.

Story continues below this ad

Is this fog the same as the smog Punjab usually witnesses in November?

No. Fog and smog are different atmospheric phenomena, although they can occur together.
Fog consists of tiny liquid water droplets suspended near the ground, while smog is polluted air containing particulate matter and gases from vehicles, industries and stubble burning. Weak winds and atmospheric stability can trap pollution near the surface, worsening air quality and visibility.

Punjab has frequently witnessed early November smog in recent years, with stubble-burning emissions adding to other sources of pollution. This November, however, the early fog is primarily linked to meteorological conditions, rather than being simply another episode of pollution-induced haze.

The two can coexist. Aerosol particles in polluted air act as cloud condensation nuclei, providing surfaces for water vapour to condense and potentially influencing fog formation and visibility, experts said.
Pal said the early fog does not necessarily signal the start of the prolonged winter fog season. It reflects a temporary convergence of favourable weather conditions, while more persistent fog episodes are usually witnessed in December and January.

Fog forms when air near the ground cools to its dew point, the temperature at which moisture in the air condenses to form water droplets. Thus, adequate moisture in the lower atmosphere is as essential as cooling.
Minimum temperatures have been below normal at several locations in Punjab, though the pattern is not uniform. According to IMD Chandigarh observations on November 19, Chandigarh recorded 10.4°C (1°C below normal), Patiala 9.3°C (-2°C), Hisar 10°C (-2°C), Narnaul 9.5°C (-2°C) and Rohtak 10.6°C (-1°C).
This variation is significant because fog is localised: dense patches can form where moisture, surface cooling and weak winds coincide, even as nearby stations record normal or above-normal temperatures.

Why counting farm fires is not enough to measure the scale of stubble burning
Surinder Pal, director, IMD Chandigarh, said moisture availability, weak winds and falling night temperatures were creating favourable conditions. The IMD’s November 19 bulletin also noted a weak western disturbance, with a trough (an elongated area of relatively low atmospheric pressure) in the middle layers of the atmosphere over eastern Afghanistan and north-west Pakistan.
Story continues below this ad
Why can fog be dense in some areas while nearby areas are clear?
While moisture provides the essential ingredient for fog, light winds and atmospheric stability determine its formation and persistence. Surinder Pal said moisture incursion, along with light north-westerly winds, was creating favourable conditions. Weak winds restrict the mixing and dispersal of air near the surface, allowing moisture to accumulate.
As the ground loses heat through radiation at night, the air above it cools. Once it reaches saturation, water vapour condenses into droplets. Stable atmospheric conditions restrict vertical mixing, allowing radiation fog to develop and persist, particularly during the night and early morning.
Local variations in humidity, irrigation, canals, agricultural fields, vegetation and surface temperatures explain why fog can be dense in isolated locations while nearby areas remain relatively clear.
Is Cyclone Akvan also influencing fog formation in north India?
The Severe Cyclonic Storm Akvan is another factor influencing the prevailing weather pattern. Surinder Pal pointed to its influence on moisture incursion. Cyclonic systems can alter atmospheric circulation and moisture movement over large areas, although Akvan should not be considered the sole or direct cause of fog in Punjab and Haryana.
Story continues below this ad
Is this fog the same as the smog Punjab usually witnesses in November?
No. Fog and smog are different atmospheric phenomena, although they can occur together.
Fog consists of tiny liquid water droplets suspended near the ground, while smog is polluted air containing particulate matter and gases from vehicles, industries and stubble burning. Weak winds and atmospheric stability can trap pollution near the surface, worsening air quality and visibility.
Punjab has frequently witnessed early November smog in recent years, with stubble-burning emissions adding to other sources of pollution. This November, however, the early fog is primarily linked to meteorological conditions, rather than being simply another episode of pollution-induced haze.
The two can coexist. Aerosol particles in polluted air act as cloud condensation nuclei, providing surfaces for water vapour to condense and potentially influencing fog formation and visibility, experts said.
Pal said the early fog does not necessarily signal the start of the prolonged winter fog season. It reflects a temporary convergence of favourable weather conditions, while more persistent fog episodes are usually witnessed in December and January.
