title: Why Telangana is scrapping intermediate colleges and merging them with schools
content_html:
The Government City College in Hyderabad. Photo: Wikimedia Commons
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The Telangana government recently decided to do away with intermediate colleges — also known as junior colleges — and replace them with Classes 11 and 12. From the next academic year (2027-28), the two grades will be integrated into the school system, with existing schools with grades up to Class 10 adding two more and conducting classes.

We explain the rationale behind the state government’s decision and how it will be implemented on the ground.

Why did the Telangana government decide to scrap Intermediate colleges?

A number of students, especially girls, drop out of the education system after passing Class 10. Students, including a majority of those hailing from socially and economically backward communities, complain of the hassle of approaching different junior colleges to get admissions.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The present system takes students through the rules and regulations of two separate education boards: School Education and Intermediate. School education up to Class 10 is managed by the School Education Department and culminates in the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) public examination conducted by the Board of Secondary Education, whereas Intermediate education is governed by the Telangana Board of Intermediate Education. Right to Education and academic activists note that the transition for students to a different type of institution after their Class 10 board exams is difficult and tiresome.

Also read | Learn German, Japanese with English: Revanth lays out plan to prepare Telangana youth for global jobs market

A few days after his government scrapped the Intermediate system, Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy, who holds the Education portfolio, said that the high dropout rate after the 10th grade was a big worrying factor. “One big reason for this is that intermediate colleges are often located far away,’’ he said. Many students from vulnerable communities who cannot afford travel and other expenses associated with attending junior colleges located far away simply discontinue education.

According to the government, about 40% of students — mostly girls and those from Dalit, tribal, and minority groups — leave school after Class 10. The dropout rates are significantly lower in institutions like Kendriya Vidyalayas, Navodaya Vidyalayas, and Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas, which offer continuous education up to the 12th grade, the government said.

How will the decision be executed at the ground level?

Story continues below this ad

In the 2025-26 batch, over 10 lakh students had enrolled in approximately 1,750 junior colleges. All the classrooms in these junior colleges will be converted and will be known as Class 11 and 12. The transition from Intermediate to School Education will affect around 11 lakh students starting next year.

As the Telangana Board of Intermediate Education will be merged with the School Education Board, the junior colleges will be used to conduct classes for 11th and 12th grades wherever possible. Schools which don’t have enough infrastructure to add more classrooms for two more grades can conduct them under the school’s name in former junior colleges located nearby. Students who pass Class 10 from a school can get admission in the same school for Classes 11 and 12 instead of searching for junior colleges.

Also read | Schools can’t collect bulk of fees upfront: Telangana human rights body orders action

The school education system will be divided into primary education (kindergarten to Class 4), secondary education (Classes 5-8), and senior secondary education (Classes 9-12).

Teachers and lecturers who are currently teaching in junior colleges will take classes for 11th and 12th grades from the next academic year. As per state Education Secretary Dr Yogita Rana, there are no changes in the syllabus, and streams like BiPC (Biology, Physics, Chemistry), MPC (Maths, Physics, Chemistry), MEC (Maths, Economics, Commerce) and CEC (Civics, Economics, Commerce) will continue. This also ensures that teachers and lecturers in junior colleges smoothly fill into roles in Classes 11 and 12, and no separate training or recruitment of new teaching staff is needed. 

What does the government aim to achieve?

Story continues below this ad

The main objective of the reforms, according to the government, is to prevent students from dropping out and ensure continuity. Students passing Class 10 often have to go through a tiring process of enrolling in junior colleges, which upsets their flow and often leaves them disoriented with the education system.

Without the hassle of seeking admissions after Class 10, students can concentrate on preparing for various competitive exams such as the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET, a pre-medical test), the Joint Entrance Examination (JEE, for admission to top engineering colleges), etc.

The quality of education also changes many times when students shift from schools to junior colleges. The scrapping of Intermediate also aims to provide quality education from the nursery level through to the university stage and prepare students to compete in the modern world and grab opportunities.

title: Two farmers were caught growing ganja. Why the one who harvested crop faces tougher charge
content_html:
Under the NDPS Act, cultivation of cannabis and possession of ganja attract different penalties, depending on the nature and quantity of the seizure. (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

On November 17, separate police parties raided two farms in villages 12 km apart in Gujarat’s Rajkot district, following tip-offs that cannabis plants were being grown there.

Growing cannabis without a licence is illegal in Gujarat, and yet some farmers take the risk.

The crop is usually harvested in November and December, keeping the police on alert. The two farmers were booked under different provisions of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act. Here’s why.

The seizures

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

A team from Vinchhiya police station in rural Rajkot raided a farm in Kharachiya Jas village and found seven cannabis plants growing amid cotton on a 2.5-bigha plot belonging to 40-year-old Paba Magan Panchala. The police uprooted the plants and seized 14.45 kg of cannabis valued at Rs 7.225 lakh. They completed the seizure by evening.

About 12 km to the west of Kharachiya Jas, the Special Operations Group (SOG) of the Rajkot Rural Police raided a farm in Chhasiya village of Vinchhiya taluka at 3 pm the same day. But the police completed their panchnama only 15 hours later, at dawn on November 18, after weighing the ganja from plants that 55-year-old Savshi Bachu Mithapara had already harvested on his five-bigha plot of land. The total seizure amounted to 705.49 kg, valued at a whopping Rs 3.52 crore.

Also in Explained | Why growing a cannabis plant in your balcony is a crime, but buying bhang isn’t

Mithapara, who had harvested the cannabis crop just four days before the police raid, was booked for possession of ganja, an offence that carries a maximum prison term of 20 years for commercial quantities. Panchala, meanwhile, was booked for cultivating cannabis, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years, regardless of the number of plants involved.

Why the difference of a decade?

The FIRs in both cases were filed at the same Vinchhiya police station.

Story continues below this ad

Paba Magan Panchala, whose cannabis plants were still standing during the police raid, was booked under Sections 8(b) and 20(a) of the NDPS Act, which prohibit and penalise the cultivation of any cannabis plant. The maximum punishment is 10 years and a fine of up to Rs 1 lakh, regardless of whether the accused cultivated one plant or an entire field.

By contrast, Savshi Bachu Mithapara, who had already harvested his crop, was booked for possession of ganja under Sections 8(c) and 20(b) of the NDPS Act. These provisions cover the production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport and use of cannabis, among other activities.

Marijuana, or weed, known as ganja in India, consists of the flowering or fruiting tops of the cannabis plant. Under the NDPS Act, seeds and leaves are excluded from this definition when they are not accompanied by these tops.

Since the quantity seized from Mithapara’s field exceeded 20 kg, the threshold for a ‘commercial quantity’ of ganja, the punishment prescribed under Section 20(b)(ii)(C) is rigorous imprisonment of at least 10 years, which may extend to 20 years, along with a fine ranging from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 2 lakh.

Why the condition of the crop matters

Story continues below this ad

There is no difference between the prescribed street value of cannabis plants and ganja decided by the Government of India. According to an October 24, 2025, notification issued by the Union Ministry of Home Affairs, all forms of ganja are valued at Rs 50,000 per kg. This is a fivefold increase from the earlier valuation of Rs 10,000 per kg, police officials confirmed.

Asked why Mithapara had been booked under the more stringent provisions of the NDPS Act despite having cultivated the crop, Inspector Fatehsingh Pargi of the Rajkot Rural SOG told The Indian Express, “The accused Mithapara had cut down the plants and set them out to dry. The number of plants could not even be counted because they had been completely dismantled branches, root and stem. So, our case is not that of cultivation of cannabis but falls in the definition of possession of ready product known as ganja.”

Also Read | Beyond Holi and bhang, the many uses of cannabis – from medicine to rope-making

Inspector AC Damor of Vinchhiya police station similarly said that Panchala had been booked for cultivation because the police found standing cannabis plants in his field, rather than a harvested product.

When is cannabis cultivation legal?

The NDPS Act generally prohibits the unauthorised cultivation of cannabis plants as well as the production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport and consumption of narcotic drugs. However, there are exceptions for cannabis, with state-level rules allowing licensed cultivation for scientific or medicinal purposes.

Story continues below this ad

Uttarakhand and Madhya Pradesh have legalised cannabis cultivation for several years. Himachal Pradesh joined them in July, permitting the controlled cultivation of cannabis for medicinal and scientific purposes.

‘We got this before GTA 6’: Why the BJP and Congress are invoking a viral meme in their political battle
content_html:
GTA 6's launch sparked a political exchange in India, with BJP highlighting the country's progress since 2013 and Congress questioning Modi's gaming imagery. (X/Narendra Modi, Rockstar Games)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The launch of Grand Theft Auto VI has given India’s political parties a new reference point in their social media messaging, with the BJP and Congress drawing on the video game’s popularity to trade political barbs.

The exchange centres on a popular internet joke about the 13-year gap between GTA V, released in 2013, and its successor, which launched worldwide on Thursday (November 19).

The BJP, including Prime Minister Narendra Modi, used the comparison to highlight what it describes as India’s progress over this period. The Congress has questioned the ruling party’s decision to associate itself with a game built around criminal activity and violence.

India is playing a whole new game! https://t.co/CMkMbK6vII

— Narendra Modi (@narendramodi) November 19, 2026

First, what is GTA?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

First released in 1997, Grand Theft Auto is an open-world video game franchise in which players explore fictional American cities, undertake missions and engage in activities ranging from driving and exploration to theft and violent crime.

Developed by Rockstar Games, the series has become known for its sprawling virtual worlds, satirical portrayal of American society and the freedom it gives players to interact with their surroundings. Its best-known instalments include GTA III, Vice City, San Andreas, GTA IV and GTA V.

Players can move freely through these virtual worlds, travelling on foot or by vehicle, and undertake missions involving everything from petty theft to organised crime. The games also recreate aspects of everyday life, including phone calls and messages, while using fictional characters and businesses to satirise American society.

MUST READ | How Grand Theft Auto changed gaming, and why GTA VI has so much to live up to

GTA VI follows Jason and Lucia, a couple involved in criminal activity in a fictionalised version of Florida. Like its predecessors, the game features violence and criminal missions alongside an expansive world that players can explore.

And what is the meme?

Story continues below this ad

The political exchange draws on a meme that became popular during the long wait for GTA VI: “We got [something] before GTA VI.” Internet users inserted major political events, technological developments and other milestones into the phrase to joke about how much had changed since the previous instalment.

The 13-year gap made the joke particularly adaptable to political messaging. For the BJP, it offered a way to present its account of changes in India since 2013 using a reference familiar to younger audiences. For the Congress, the game’s criminal themes provided an opportunity to ridicule the Prime Minister’s choice of imagery.

The franchise’s popularity added to the attention surrounding the exchange. Rockstar Games, the game’s publisher, said GTA VI generated $3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, describing it as the biggest entertainment launch in history.

How has the BJP used GTA VI?

As anticipation surrounding the game’s release grew, the Prime Minister’s X and Instagram accounts published a series of slides borrowing the franchise’s distinctive typography and imagery.

Story continues below this ad

“Between GTA V and VI, here’s how India upgraded”, the post stated, followed by images of ‘Level Up’ across various sectors from the economy and poverty alleviation to ramping up its solar power generation capacity and start-up ecosystem.

Also Read | GTA 6, Modi and the BJP’s bid to crack the Gen Z audience

The campaign used the period between the two releases to showcase the government’s claims about India’s economic growth, infrastructure development and other achievements.

According to BJP sources, the party’s social media workers had identified the trend before the game’s launch. However, the decision to capitalise on it was made following Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi’s recent interaction with students at US universities.

On Saturday (November 21), Minister of Road Transport and Highways Nitin Gadkari’s social media account used similar imagery to highlight highway construction and reductions in travel time across the country.

Story continues below this ad

Several BJP state units and accounts associated with senior leaders, including Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, also amplified the trend.

Why has the Congress objected?

The Congress attacked the Prime Minister’s choice of imagery, pointing to the game’s central themes of crime and violence.

Congress communications in-charge Jairam Ramesh criticised the Prime Minister’s post, referring to GTA VI’s protagonists, Jason and Lucia, who are involved in criminal activity. He said in a post, “The PM in a desperate bid to reach out to the youth has resorted to GTA V and GTA VI imagery on social media. Recall that this video game follows a criminal duo. How very appropriate.”

The BJP responded by accusing the Congress of focusing on the video game’s storyline rather than engaging with the figures presented in Modi’s post.

Story continues below this ad

BJP social media co-convenor Priti Gandhi said the post was “about exposing Congress-era failures & showcasing India’s progress” since 2014. “You were unable to counter a single figure, so you chose to moralise about video-game characters…” she alleged.

The Congress also circulated a minute-long video highlighting the game’s violent themes, captioned “From Vote Chori To GTA: Modi’s Perfect Match”.

content_html:
Travel insurance has also become an increasingly popular tool for travellers to safeguard against losses arising from travel disruptions. (AP)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

When it comes to insurance, claims and settlements happen to be the most important metrics. Data from Asego, a global travel assistance and insurance provider, showed that non-medical claims account for over two-thirds of travel insurance claims in the first nine months of the financial year but just a fifth of total payouts.

Payouts are much better for medical claims, which account for just a third of travel insurance claims but make up 80% of total payouts. The data is based on Asego’s analysis of nearly 11,000 travel insurance claims.

“The analysis brings out two distinct dimensions of travel risk: the frequency of everyday travel disruptions and the potentially substantial financial consequences of medical emergencies,” noted Dev Karvat, Founder and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Asego.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

So, why is there such disparity between medical and non-medical claim settlements, and what does this data show us?

Why are non-medical claims so frequent?

Non-medical claims consist of issues such as flight cancellations, delays, baggage issues, and stolen belongings, among others. These are very common while travelling, leading to a substantially higher number of claims.

“Flight delays, cancellations, baggage delays, and missed connections are more commonly experienced by travellers. However, the individual payouts are generally smaller and subject to policy limits,” said Ramit Goyal, Chief Distribution Officer at Generali Central Insurance.

Explained | Why everything from flight tickets to pen drives is getting more expensive

A changing global order has also led to higher claims. “Weather disruptions, airline operational issues, geopolitical developments, and complex flight itineraries have increased travellers’ exposure to non-medical risks, contributing to higher claim volumes in these categories,” Goyal added.

Story continues below this ad

The Asego report noted that travel delays and cancellations were the biggest reason for non-medical claims, accounting for 27%. Trip cancellations accounted for 23% of the claims, while delayed baggage contributed to 14%.

“While these incidents may not always involve large individual payouts, their frequency makes them a significant component of travel insurance claims,” said Asego’s Dev Karvat.

Behind the payout gap

While non-medical claims are more frequent, they often cost less to resolve than medical claims.

“The data reflects a fundamental insurance principle — the most frequent claims are not necessarily the most expensive. A relatively small number of high-value medical claims can account for a significant proportion of total payouts,” said Goyal.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | Why Mumbai airport plans to shift flights to Navi Mumbai by destination, not airline

Healthcare costs are much higher in many international destinations, leading to medical claim payouts ballooning despite a lower number of claims.

Asego’s findings also show the same. According to the company, consolidated data from insurers showed that total cashless and reimbursement payouts between April and November were at $6.7 million, out of which medical claims accounted for $5.3 million and non-medical at $1.3 million.

“The data highlights how a relatively smaller proportion of medical incidents can translate into a significantly higher financial burden,” the report said.

Travel insurance has also become an increasingly popular tool for travellers to safeguard against losses arising from travel disruptions. This popularity is also behind a higher number of non-medical claims, which are more frequent, as per industry executives.

Story continues below this ad

“Travel insurance has now become much more widespread. People are slowly getting how a small amount can save you in case of major mishaps. Thus, higher claims are a part and parcel of this increased attention,” noted an industry executive.

title: Price of war: How India’s oil, gas import bill is soaring amid West Asia crisis
content_html:
In October, the last month for which data is available, the oil import bill jumped 87.5% on-year to $19.5 billion. (Reuters Photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

India’s crude oil import bill surged by nearly 54% on a year-on-year (y-o-y) basis in the first seven months of the current financial year, even as import volumes rose only slightly amid supply tightness and elevated prices owing to the West Asia conflict and the consequent Strait of Hormuz crisis, as per provisional data from the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas (MoPNG).

Elevated prices also led to a jump in liquefied natural gas (LNG) import bill and fuel export value. As a result, net oil and gas imports — arrived at by deducting petroleum product exports from oil, natural gas, and petroleum product imports — were higher by almost 40% from the year-ago levels, underscoring the adverse economic impact of the West Asia crisis on energy import-dependent India.

The country depends on imports to meet over 88% of its crude oil requirement and about half of its consumption of natural gas, which is imported as LNG, or super-chilled gas. Despite depending on imported oil and gas, India is a net exporter of petroleum products due to its massive oil refining capacity, while it also imports some petroleum products like liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Prior to the West Asia war, which broke out in late-February, about 40% of India’s crude oil imports, 60% of its LNG imports, and a whopping 90% of its LPG imports came from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz.

Also Read | India’s Russian fossil fuel imports at record high of €6.4 billion in October amid elevated prices

Although the physical supply tightness — a key worry in the first few months of the war — has now eased to a large extent, energy prices remain elevated and volatile amid sky-high freight and insurance costs owing to war risk premiums. After moderating slightly in June-August, oil prices jumped again in September-October as a result of renewed hostility in West Asia and soaring freight costs. In October alone, India’s oil import bill surged by nearly 88% y-o-y.

India has been forced to import oil and gas at extremely high rates as the country has been prioritising supply security over price considerations, given its extreme reliance on imports and largely inelastic demand.

India’s oil and gas trade math

According to latest provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) of the MoPNG, crude oil imports in April-October jumped 53.5% y-o-y to $111 billion, even as import volumes rose by just 2.7% to 146.6 million tonnes, or about 1.08 billion barrels.

Story continues below this ad

This translates to about $103.3 per barrel as the average landed price of imported crude oil in the seven-month period, up from around $69 per barrel in the corresponding period of last year. The April-October oil import bill is already 88% of the import value for the full financial year 2025-26, and there are still five months to go in the current fiscal.

War impact on India’s oil, gas import bill.

In October, the last month for which data is available, the oil import bill jumped 87.5% y-o-y to $19.5 billion. The Indian crude oil basket averaged at $116.1 per barrel in September and $119.9 per barrel in October. It stood at $114.48 in April, $106.2 in May, $83.2 in June, $82 in July, and $90.2 in August.

As for LNG imports, while supplies rose 7.4% to 22,175 million standard cubic metres (mscm) in April-October, the LNG import bill rose by 35.8% to $11 billion, reflecting the spurt in prices. Petroleum product imports almost halved in volume terms to 15.1 million tonnes from 29.8 million tonnes, as supply of major petroleum products that India imports — like LPG — were impacted by the war. In value terms, the decline in petroleum product imports was relatively lower — down 25% to $9.9 billion — due to super-normal prices in the international market.

Also Read | Goods exports log all-time high of $50 billion in October, trade gap at year’s peak

India’s petroleum product export volumes declined 13.5% to 32.1 million tonnes in April-October as domestic fuel supplies took precedence amid the global supply crunch. Nonetheless, the exports surged 47% in value to $34.1 billion due to the jump in international petroleum fuel prices.

Story continues below this ad

Taking into account the overall oil, LNG, and petroleum product imports as well as fuel exports, the country’s net oil and gas imports rose 39% y-o-y in April-October to $97.7 billion, PPAC data shows.

India’s concerns

Energy imports are a major component of India’s overall imports, and any meaningful increase has ramifications for the country’s trade balance, current account, inflation, and the rupee’s exchange rate, among others. For instance, India’s wholesale fuel and power inflation was 32.8% in October, 25.9% in September, and 23.2% in August, as per government data.

Also Read | The ethanol mirage: Why E100 won’t Solve India’s oil import problems

The country imports 1.8-2 billion barrels of oil a year, and every $1-per-barrel increase in price bumps up its oil import bill by up to $2 billion on an annualised basis. According to a March report by Nomura, India is among the three Asian economies most vulnerable to high oil prices. It also said that every 10% increase in oil price typically widens the country’s current account deficit by 0.4% on the gross domestic product (GDP). Crude oil alone is the country’s largest merchandise import.

Heavy dependence on energy imports has led to a double whammy of supply tightness and price surge. While highly diversified crude sourcing has helped in ensuring adequate oil, petrol, diesel, and jet fuel availability amid the West Asia crisis, some rationing of gas supplies to certain industries and commercial consumers was done in the initial months of the conflict in order to ensure adequate availability for households and a few priority sectors.

title: As India Inc posts record Q2 profit, why top five companies made up a quarter
content_html:
While Indian companies historically get the heat for not reinvesting enough into their businesses and instead hold on to large piles of cash and pay out substantial dividends, data shows that these companies may finally be spending these increased earnings on capital expenditure.
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

India Inc reported record profit during second quarter of the financial year 2027 (Q2FY27), outperforming the Street’s expectations. This comes despite the challenges, which included high raw material costs across most industries due to the ongoing West Asia war.

The 2,600-odd listed companies tracked by the Bank of Baroda reported a record net profit of around Rs 4.5 lakh crore during Q2FY27, up nearly 26% year-on-year (y-o-y). The net sales of these companies grew 21% to around Rs 36 lakh crore, said Aditi Gupta, an economist at the bank.

So, who is making the most money among these companies, and where is the cash going?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Who makes money?

Reliance Industries Ltd earned the most profit in the Indian listed space, with its oil business boosting its net profit for the July-September quarter to a record Rs 29,550 crore. State Bank of India’s net profit came in at Rs 23,038 crore. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd reported a profit of Rs 21,630 crore, a sharp reversal from the Rs 2,661 crore loss in the previous quarter.

HDFC Bank Ltd and Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd reported profits of Rs 19,510 crore and Rs 18,538 crore.

Net profit of top five companies.

Together, the top five accounted for a quarter of India Inc’s total profits.

Collectively, the top 10, which also consists of ICICI Bank Ltd, Tata Consultancy Services Ltd, LIC, Bharti Airtel Ltd, and Infosys Ltd, accounted for 38% of India Inc’s profits and nearly 47% of its revenues.

Story continues below this ad

In fact, the top 50 companies, or Nifty 50, make up around 55% of India Inc’s total profits, highlighting that only a handful of companies are driving aggregate profit to record levels. The pace of profit growth was strong all around, with earnings of Nifty 50 companies growing at around 27% y-o-y, while Motilal Oswal’s coverage universe of around 400 companies saw around 32% growth.

Also Read | India Inc’s Budget wish list: Targeted sops, LTCG tax cut, R&D in focus

The growth has been driven by higher volumes across most sectors such as automobiles, banking, and oil, even as margins remain under pressure due to higher costs in the wake of the war in West Asia.

Banks, financial services companies, and oil exploration companies were among the top performers during the quarter, as a high interest rate environment and high crude oil prices proved to be tailwinds. In fact, in the first half of FY27, the profitability of public-sector banks jumped 17% y-o-y to a record Rs 1.1 lakh crore.

Where the cash is going

While Indian companies historically get the heat for not reinvesting enough into their businesses and instead hold on to large piles of cash and pay out substantial dividends, data shows that these companies may finally be spending these increased earnings on capital expenditure. As per Emkay Global, operating cash flow to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA) ratio of top 500 BSE companies fell to 64% in first half of FY26 from nearly 83% in FY26 and well below the 78-83% seen across FY22-26. This meant companies had lower free cash on their books compared to their operating profit.  “The weakness was concentrated in the cyclicals. Discretionary (25.4% vs 68.0% in FY26), industrials (44.3%), and materials (42.9%). Energy (82.9% vs 106.5%) also moderated,” the report said.

Story continues below this ad

“Some of this is likely due to working-capital build-up in a high-growth phase, and half-year ratios are not strictly comparable with full-year ones; even so, this is the number to track in 2HFY27,” it added.

While this does not mean that cash is being reinvested, as companies also pay out large dividends, data shows that capital expenditure from corporate sector has been picking up in recent times.

While official data for FY27 is not yet out, the Reserve Bank of India’s projections show that private corporate investment may rise about 23% to Rs 3.2 lakh crore in FY27. title: Anthropic’s stock market debut marks many firsts. Will it boost a struggling AI sector?
content_html:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind Claude, priced its IPO at $83 a share when it listed on the Nasdaq, well above the expected range, and ended up selling far more shares than planned. The company has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5 trillion as its shares are set to start trading from Thursday, already making it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

There are many other interesting firsts. Anthropic’s stock market debut will make it the first wholly AI-focused company to go public, at a time when the fast-growing sector faces multiple questions over the amount of money being poured into the technology.

What is remarkable is that this company has been in existence for just around five years. And to put the listing performance in perspective, Anthropic’s valuation is already more than the cumulative market cap of the top 10 Indian companies.

How big is Anthropic’s stock market debut?

The listing would mean Anthropic’s seven co-founders are set to become ‘decabillionaires’ (wealth exceeding $10 billion). Since Anthropic’s shares were oversubscribed to the tune of more than 10 times ahead of the listing, its valuation could surge past its target when trading kicks off Thursday.

That means Anthropic could surge past the early market valuation of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which was the world’s most highly valued market debut in June when it listed with a value of over $2.2 trillion. SpaceX shares fell significantly shortly after the listing, bringing down its valuation. The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX had raised in June, according to Bloomberg data.

Anthropic said in its filing that Amazon, Google and Microsoft “simultaneously serve as our investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors.” That is generally a very rare situation, in any business. Rival OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, meanwhile, is expected to go public next year.

“Anthropic, an AI company known for Claude, listed at a valuation of $ 1.5 trillion. It did not exist till ~ 5 years ago. This is more than the combined market cap of the top 10 Indian companies. Are we undervalued, or do we need to catch up in the new world? Or both?,” Uday Kotak, the Executive Vice Chairman and Managing Director of Kotak Mahindra Bank said in a post on X.

Can Anthropic’s IPO boost confidence in the AI sector?

An industry analyst said while the biggest IPO ever is being done by a model (large language model) company and not a hardware one, the billion dollar question is how much of that money would be directed straight into compute (data centres, which is essentially hardware)

This also comes at a time when this sector has struggled to tackle what has been its biggest bugbear: monetisation. “I think they (AI companies) are thrashing around for revenue ideas,” a US-based technology analyst told The Indian Express.

The path to monetisation is a struggle, despite companies such as Anthropic doing better on the B2B (business-to-business) side. “That’s the story that Anthropic is doing better in enterprise. They do distribute more widely through all the CSPs (cloud service providers).”

title: Power shortage looms: Why states are flocking to spot market as coal stocks dip
content_html:
India faces growing power shortage concerns as declining coal stocks and inadequate thermal capacity raise questions over electricity supply ahead of next summer. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

A looming power shortage, triggered by a shortage of baseload thermal capacity and mounting worries over coal stocks, has spurred a flurry of high-level meetings at the Centre.

With the states now being directed to secure electricity at all costs, the worries about an impending electricity shock early next summer have triggered a panic reaction that is reverberating across the country’s electricity ecosystem.

Multiple states are turning to short-term power procurement tenders, mostly at exorbitant prices, to secure additional electricity for the coming months and guard against potential shortages, particularly during evening peak hours.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Data from the Ministry of Power’s DEEP (Discovery of Efficient Electricity Price) portal showed that tenders have been floated for power procurement by at least five states and private distribution utilities for additional power during the months of January, February, March, April, May and June-July next year. The states seeking to procure additional power include Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Rajasthan and Gujarat.

Uttar Pradesh is also learnt to be vying for securing additional power ahead of the state elections early next year.

Here is why power prices are surging in short-term tenders, how sharply coal stocks have depleted at thermal plants, and what past policy missteps left the grid vulnerable.

Why power prices are soaring in short-term tenders

Private distribution companies, including Noida Power Company Ltd and Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd (AEML), have also floated tenders. Prices discovered in some of these tenders have touched Rs 19-20 per unit, significantly higher than the price caps applicable in power exchanges.

Story continues below this ad
Also in Explained | FPIs pump record $11.3 billion in November: What drove this comeback?

While the cap on spot prices is Rs 10 per unit, prices can go up to Rs 20 per unit in the specialised High Price Day-Ahead Market (HP-DAM). Also, amid a decline in coal stocks, the government is also discussing measures to expand coal storage capacity at thermal power plants beyond the prescribed normative requirement, The Indian Express has learnt.

While the normative requirement is around 59 million tonnes (mt), thermal power plants currently have the capacity to store up to 80 mt, equivalent to about 30 days of consumption. Discussions are also underway on doubling this capacity to 160 mt, which would provide up to 60 days of coal stocks. However, such an expansion would require additional storage space at thermal power plants.

While sporadic instances of rains may have helped mitigate the shortage this year, there are concerns about a problem from early next summer. Grid India’s daily frequency profile data is showing even during these somewhat lean demand months real-time frequency is falling to below the mandated lower limit of 49.9 HZ even during solar hours (when solar generation is available). The situation during the non-solar hours (evenings, when solar generation is not available) is even more precipitous.

Coal stocks at thermal plants fall sharply, raising shortage fears

Story continues below this ad

The increased dependence on coal-based generation has put pressure on coal inventories at thermal power plants. Stocks declined by around 66% between April and September this year, compared with a fall of around 23% during the same period last year, when inventories dropped from 55.2 mt at the beginning of April to 42.6 mt by September end.

The corresponding declines during the same period were 31.8% in 2024 and 36.8% in 2023.

As of November 15, coal inventory at domestic coal-based power plants stood at 20.79 mt, down from around 55 mt at the beginning of April. Officials in the Ministry of Power have also maintained that rebuilding coal stocks ahead of next summer is among the key priorities given the current circumstances.

The fresh directive to ramp up coal storage capacity comes in this backdrop.

Story continues below this ad

How past policy decisions left India vulnerable to a power crunch

Internally, the Union Power Ministry’s planning body — the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) — has already given a broader call for a reassessment of planned coal-based capacity additions, even as the country continues to expand its renewable energy capacity.

Also Read | ‘Very wrong signal to investors’: Behind Vedanta’s Anil Agarwal’s message to govt on ONGC transfer

With India staring at a power shortage, CEA chairperson Ghanshyam Prasad had flagged the need to to add 105-150 gigawatts (GW) of coal-based power capacity by 2035, significantly higher than the 97 GW currently planned, at a meeting on October 13.

India’s focus on rapid expansion of renewables in the absence of energy storage systems is making the electricity grid increasingly unstable. The issue is compounded by a policy decision from around ten years ago to scale down thermal expansion, which provides critical baseload support to the grid during evenings in summer months, when solar generation dips and demand remains high.

The Union Power Ministry’s National Electricity Plan (2017-22) had ruled out fresh thermal capacity additions beyond 2022, apart from the 50 GW of under-construction projects. It mainly focused on scaling up renewables. Additionally, imported coal-based projects were actively discouraged, primarily in the wake of spiralling global coal prices.

Story continues below this ad

Since the planning misstep of 2016-17, some corrective measures have been taken: a renewed push for nuclear generation in fleet mode, a belated drive to add large thermal capacities, importing coal to restart idle plants, and renewed policy pivots such as the CEA’s directive from last year that mandated storage for all new solar projects.
